title: Self Coding Agents — Colin Flaherty, Augment Code

summary: Colin Flaherty of Augment Code describes the company's journey building an AI coding agent that largely wrote itself, with over 90% of its ~20,000-line codebase generated by the agent under human supervision. The agent implemented core features such as third-party integrations (Slack, Linear, Jira, Notion, Google Search), wrote unit tests, and performed self-optimization by profiling its own code, identifying synchronous file-loading bottlenecks, and adding a process pool with stress tests. Notably, the agent used a Google Search integration it had previously written to look up Linear API documentation, then implemented the Linear integration from those docs. Flaherty identifies three foundational pillars: a scalable enterprise-ready context engine, best-in-class foundation model reasoning, and a safe code execution environment. He corrects several common assumptions: agents are not yet at senior-engineer level despite social media demos, professional software engineering is rarely zero-to-one, and environments are messier than demos show. He recommends thinking in terms of complexity levels rather than task categories, since the technology is general-purpose, and warns against anthropomorphizing agents. A key innovation is the knowledge base concept—markdown files that patch gaps in model knowledge without retraining. Flaherty draws an analogy between onboarding agents and onboarding new hires. The agent also uses a memory tool to continuously learn from human interactions. In the latter part of the talk, Flaherty explores how cheap code changes product development: when engineering hours are no longer the bottleneck, the focus shifts to product insights and design. Context is multiplicative—access to both codebase and Slack is far more useful than either alone. The agent handled non-coding SDLC tasks like generating PR summaries posted to Slack and plotting its own lines of code over time. Flaherty shares a hard-to-test race condition bug the agent introduced in a cache save function, underscoring the importance of sufficient tests. On an internal bug-fixing benchmark, upgrading the foundation model by six months yielded a 4% improvement, but adding the ability for the agent to iteratively run tests and suggest fixes yielded a 20% gain. Better tests enable more autonomy. He concludes that agents are now compounding—helping build themselves—and that good test harnesses matter more than ever, while the bottleneck shifts from writing code to gathering customer feedback and building product insights.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

The agent self-optimized: it profiled its own code, found synchronous bottlenecks, and added a process pool with stress tests
When code is cheap to write, the bottleneck shifts from engineering hours to product insights, design, and customer feedback

sections.title: Introduction and Agent Overview
sections.summary: Flaherty introduces himself and Augment Code, traces the evolution from autocomplete (2023) to chat models (2024) to agents (2025), and reveals the agent codebase has ~20,000 lines with over 90% written by the agent under human supervision.

sections.title: Self-Building: Integrations, Tests, and Self-Optimization
sections.summary: Describes the agent implementing third-party integrations, using its own Google search tool to look up Linear API docs, writing unit tests with process management tools, and profiling itself to find and fix a synchronous file-loading bottleneck by adding a process pool and stress test.

sections.title: Live Demonstrations
sections.summary: Walks through examples: agent confirming Google search, instrumenting its own search tool with logs, running a sub-copy of itself, detecting missing credentials and using clarify and memory tools, and returning example log output. Highlights the critical role of the context engine.

sections.title: Foundations and Common Assumptions
sections.summary: Identifies three pillars (context engine, foundation model reasoning, code execution environment). Corrects misconceptions: agents aren't at senior level, professional engineering is rarely zero-to-one, think in complexity levels not task categories, and don't anthropomorphize agents.

sections.title: Knowledge Base and Agent Onboarding
sections.summary: Introduces knowledge base concept—markdown files patching model knowledge gaps (e.g., graphite commands). Draws analogy between onboarding agents and new hires. Notes that agents enabled parallel iteration on multiple third-party integrations simultaneously.

sections.title: Product Development, Testing, and the Future of Software Engineering
sections.summary: Explores how cheap code shifts the bottleneck to product insights and design. Context is multiplicative. Agent handled non-coding SDLC tasks like PR announcements and plotting its own codebase growth. Shares a race condition bug the agent introduced in a cache save function, underscoring the need for sufficient tests. Reports that iterative test-run-fix loops yielded a 20% benchmark gain vs. 4% from a model upgrade. Concludes that agents are compounding by helping build themselves, and good test harnesses matter more than ever.

demonstrations: Agent confirms Google search capability and returns example results
Agent instruments its own Google search tool with logs by using retrieval to find the file, editing it, and running a sub-copy of itself
Agent detects missing Google credentials, uses clarify tool to ask the user, then uses memory tool to remember credential location
Agent used Google search integration it wrote to look up Linear API docs, then implemented Linear integration
Agent profiled itself by adding print statements, running sub-copies, finding synchronous file-loading bottleneck, and adding process pool with stress test
Knowledge base enabled agent to use graphite stacking-PR commands after reading a markdown file
Agent generated announcement of latest PRs and posted it to Slack
Agent made a plot of interactive agent lines of code as a function of date
limitations: Foundation models have not memorized some tools and APIs (e.g., graphite, Linear API docs)
Agents are not yet at senior software engineering level despite demos suggesting otherwise
Agents can miss hard-to-test issues like race conditions in parallel cache writes
Professional software engineering environments are messier than Twitter demos show
Agents cannot be retrained overnight on new tools by the user
Insufficient test coverage allows agent-introduced bugs to slip through
